Your pitch over the last 8 seconds

Within 10 cents counts as in tune; a semitone is 100 cents.

Sing an open vowel like "ah" in a quiet room. Hold the phone about an arm's length away.

Reference notes now ring for about as long as you need to hold a note steady (around a third of a second), and the tone itself has a softer, more piano-like strike and decay.

In Sequence and Memory mode, matching now accepts anything closer to the target note than to its neighbors (within half a semitone) and is octave-flexible — singing the right note an octave higher or lower than the reference still counts as correct. A brief wobble off-pitch no longer resets your progress to zero; it just eases back a bit, so natural vibrato won't keep you from confirming a note you're actually holding.

The microphone is paused while the app plays its own reference notes, so it doesn't mistake them for your singing or your piano. Wait for "your turn", or tick the headphones box if you're wearing headphones. The line under the verdict tells you what the mic is hearing: too quiet, or sound without a clear pitch. For a real piano, play one note at a time and let it ring.

Piano sound: recorded grand piano samples from the MusyngKite soundfont (via midi-js-soundfonts), licensed Creative Commons BY-SA 3.0.

Pitch tolerance controls how close you need to be. It starts on Very forgiving (up to about three-quarters of a semitone off still counts in Sequence and Memory mode); the green zone on the dial grows and shrinks to show exactly what counts. A brief wobble off-pitch now only slowly drains your hold progress, so vibrato won't keep resetting it. The cents readout under the dial shows how far you are from the note you're aiming for.

When Sequence mode is set to Play as chord, you can sing the notes back in any order — whichever of the chord's notes you're closest to is the one being checked, and each gets marked off as you hit it. Switch to Play one by one if you'd rather practice singing them back in the exact order they were played.

Reference notes now ring out for a couple of seconds — longer, fuller, and deeper, with more low-end body and a longer natural decay — without requiring you to hold your own note any longer than before. The piano tone also has a touch of room ambience and tiny natural pitch variation between notes, so it sounds a little less like a synthesizer and a little more like a real instrument.

In Sequence mode, play the notes as a chord or one by one, then sing them back in order — each circle turns into a check once you hold that note steady for a moment, and the app moves you to the next one.

Set the length to 1 for a single-note trainer, or 3 for a chord trainer. Tap 🎲 Random note(s) to get a fresh pick from the piano's two center octaves — it plays right away, and you can tap Play sequence any time to hear it again. Turn on Auto-continue to get a brand new random note or chord automatically each time you complete one.

Memory mode is built for people who lose earlier notes as soon as they hear a new one. It starts with a single note; each time you sing it back correctly, it replays everything so far plus one new note, and you sing the whole chain from the start. This forces you to actually retain each pitch rather than only the most recent one — a normal skill to build, and it improves with repetition.
